# Target
The compiled C++ binary is /workspace/dataset/test5_executable .
Its source (the test driver only) is /workspace/dataset/test5.cpp :

    if (argc < 2) return 1;
    std::string url = argv[1];
    url_parser::URL parser(url);
    std::cout << parser.scheme() << std::endl;   // line 1
    std::cout << parser.host()   << std::endl;   // line 2
    std::cout << parser.port()   << std::endl;   // line 3  (an integer; -1 when absent)
    std::cout << parser.path()   << std::endl;   // line 4
    std::cout << parser.query()  << std::endl;   // line 5

So EVERY successful run prints exactly 5 newline-terminated lines. Empty fields print as empty lines.
The library source is NOT available and you must NOT try to find or read it. Pure black-box probing.

# How to probe (IMPORTANT)
Run it like:
    /workspace/dataset/test5_executable 'THE_URL'
To see exact bytes including empty trailing lines, ALWAYS capture with a delimiter, e.g.:
    /workspace/dataset/test5_executable 'http://a.com' | sed -n 'l' ; echo "exit=${PIPESTATUS[0]}"
or the most reliable formatting for reporting — number every line:
    /workspace/dataset/test5_executable 'http://a.com' | cat -A | nl -ba
Use single quotes around the URL. For URLs containing single quotes, control characters, or
non-UTF8 bytes, use perl to exec with an exact argv, e.g.:
    perl -e 'exec("/workspace/dataset/test5_executable", "http://a\x27b.com")' | cat -A | nl -ba
Batch many probes in ONE bash call with a loop so you use few tool calls, e.g.:
    for u in 'http://a' 'http://a:1' 'a://b'; do printf '=== [%s]\n' "$u"; /workspace/dataset/test5_executable "$u" | cat -A | nl -ba; done
`cat -A` renders end-of-line as `$`, tabs as `^I`, so an empty field shows as a line containing only `$`.
Probe generously — dozens to hundreds of inputs. It is cheap. Note python3 is NOT installed; perl is.
Do not write anything into /workspace/dataset or /output. Use /tmp for scratch files.

# What to report
Report the OBSERVED FACTS, not guesses. For each rule you state, cite at least one concrete
input and its exact 5 field values. If two plausible rules both explain your data, say so and
design a discriminating probe, then run it. Be exhaustive within your assigned dimension.


Dimension: DELIMITER PRECEDENCE and cross-field interactions — the combinatorics.
The parser presumably scans for ':', '/', '?', '#', '@' in some order. Your job is to determine
the exact ORDER of operations by probing inputs where the delimiters appear in unusual relative
positions. Systematically probe inputs of the form 'http://HOSTPART' where HOSTPART contains the
delimiters in every interesting order, e.g.:
'http://a/b:c', 'http://a?b:c', 'http://a#b:c', 'http://a:1/b:2', 'http://a/b?c:d',
'http://a?b/c', 'http://a#b/c', 'http://a#b?c', 'http://a?b#c', 'http://a/b#c?d',
'http://a:1?b/c', 'http://a:1#b/c', 'http://a@b:1/c?d#e', 'http://a:1@b:2/c?d#e',
'http://a/b@c', 'http://a?b@c', 'http://a:1/2:3?4:5#6:7'.
KEY questions to answer definitively with evidence:
 (a) Is the ':' searched for the port limited to the authority segment (before the first '/'),
     or does a ':' later in the path get mistaken for a port?
 (b) Is the '?' searched over the whole string or only after the path start?
 (c) Does a '#' before a '?' prevent the query from being found?
 (d) Is '@' handled at all (userinfo stripping)?
Also probe a full-featured URL 'https://user:pw@sub.example.co.uk:8443/a/b/c.html?x=1&y=2#frag'
and report all five fields exactly.

content.text: All probes complete. The pipeline is fully determined.

input.dimension: DELIMITER PRECEDENCE and cross-field interactions (order of operations for '#', '?', '://', '/', '@', ':')

rules.rule: STEP 1 (first of all): the fragment is truncated at the FIRST '#' in the RAW input, before anything else is parsed. Everything from '#' onward is discarded and never appears in any of the 5 fields.
rules.evidence: 'http://a#b?c' -> scheme=http, host=a, port=-1, path='', query='' (the '?c' is gone). 'http://a/b#c?d' -> http / a / -1 / '/b' / '' (query empty even though a '?' exists after the '#'). 'http://a##b' -> http / a / -1 / '' / '' (first '#' wins).

rules.rule: The '#' truncation happens even before scheme detection, so a '#' occurring earlier in the string than '://' destroys the scheme and host entirely.

STEP 2: the query is split off at the FIRST '?' of the fragment-stripped string, searched over the WHOLE string — this happens BEFORE scheme/authority/path parsing. query = everything after that '?'; the remainder (everything before it) is what the rest of the parser sees.
rules.evidence: 'a?://b' -> scheme='', host='', port=-1, path='a', query='://b'. If '://' were found first the scheme would have been 'a?' and host 'b'; instead the '?' split ran first, leaving 'a' (no '://') as a bare path. Same for 'a?b://c' -> ''/''/-1/'a'/'b://c' and 'http?://a' -> ''/''/-1/'http'/'://a' and 'x?y://u:p@h:9/p?q' -> ''/''/-1/'x'/'y://u:p@h:9/p?q'.

rules.rule: Because the '?' split precedes everything, a '?' anywhere before the authority makes the query swallow the rest of the URL verbatim, including further '://', '@', ':' and '/' characters, which are NOT re-parsed.
Only the FIRST '?' is a delimiter; subsequent '?' characters are ordinary query bytes.
A trailing '?' yields an empty query, indistinguishable from no '?' at all in the 5-field output.
rules.evidence: 'http://a?' -> http / a / -1 / '' / ''; identical to 'http://a' -> http / a / -1 / '' / ''. Also 'http://a?#b' -> http / a / -1 / '' / ''.

rules.rule: STEP 3: the scheme is found by searching the (fragment- and query-stripped) remainder for the FIRST literal three-character sequence '://'. scheme = everything before it, lowercased; the parse continues after it. There is NO character-set validation of the scheme — '/', '@', ':', space are all accepted inside it.
rules.evidence: 'a/b://c' -> scheme='a/b', host='c'. 'a@b://c' -> scheme='a@b', host='c'. 'ht:tp://a' -> scheme='ht:tp', host='a'. ':a://b' -> scheme=':a', host='b'. '/a://b' -> scheme='/a', host='b'. ' http://a.com ' -> scheme=' http', host='a.com ' (no trimming). 'HTTP://A.COM/B?C' -> scheme='http' (lowercased) but host='A.COM' (case preserved). 'a://b://c' -> scheme='a', host='b', path='//c' (first '://' wins).

rules.rule: If '://' is absent from the remainder, the parser takes a completely different branch: scheme='', host='', port=-1, and the ENTIRE remainder becomes the path — '/', ':' and '@' inside it are not parsed at all.
An empty scheme before '://' is legal and takes the authority branch.
rules.evidence: '://a' -> scheme='', host='a', port=-1, path='', query=''. '://' -> ''/''/-1/''/''. Contrast with the no-'://' branch above where host is empty AND path holds the text.

rules.rule: STEP 4: in the post-'://' remainder, the authority ends at the FIRST '/'. path = that '/' and everything after it (leading '/' always retained); if no '/' exists, path is empty. All remaining '/' characters are just path bytes.
rules.evidence: 'http://a//b' -> http / a / -1 / '//b' / ''. 'http://a///b?c' -> http / a / -1 / '///b' / 'c'. 'http:////a' -> http / '' / -1 / '//a' / '' (authority is the empty string before the first '/'). 'http:///a' -> http / '' / -1 / '/a' / ''. 'http://a/' -> http / a / -1 / '/' / ''. 'http://a/?b' -> http / a / -1 / '/' / 'b'.

rules.rule: ANSWER TO (b): '?' is searched over the whole string, NOT only after the path start. The query can be non-empty with an empty path, and a '?' preceding the first '/' prevents any path from being found.
ANSWER TO (c): YES — a '#' before a '?' completely prevents the query from being found, because the '#' truncation is step 1.
rules.evidence: 'http://a#b?c' -> query=''. 'http://a#?b' -> query=''. 'http://a#b?c#d' -> query=''. 'http://a#b/c?d:e@f' -> http / a / -1 / '' / ''. 'x://#?a' i.e. 'http://#?a' -> http / '' / -1 / '' / ''. Reverse order works: 'http://a?b#c' -> query='b'.

rules.rule: ANSWER TO (d): YES, '@' userinfo stripping IS implemented, but only inside the authority segment, and it splits at the FIRST '@' (not the last, unlike RFC 3986). The text before the first '@' is discarded; the remainder — including any further '@' — becomes the host[:port] string with no re-scan.
rules.evidence: 'http://a@b@c' -> host='b@c' (RFC would give host 'c'). 'http://a@b@c@d' -> host='b@c@d'. 'http://a@b@c:1/d' -> host='b@c', port=1. 'http://a@@b:9' -> host='@b', port=9. 'http://@@a:9' -> host='@a', port=9. 'http://@@' i.e. 'http://@@' -> host='@'.

rules.rule: The '@' search is confined to the authority (i.e. before the first '/' and before the first '?'/'#', which were already removed). An '@' in the path or query is an ordinary byte and never triggers userinfo stripping.
'@' is stripped BEFORE the port colon is looked for, so a ':' in the userinfo (a password) is never mistaken for a port, and the port comes from the post-'@' part.
rules.evidence: 'http://:1@a' -> host='a', port=-1 (the ':1' was userinfo, not a port). 'http://a:1@b' -> host='b', port=-1. 'http://a:1@b:2/c?d#e' -> host='b', port=2. 'http://u:p@a:1' -> host='a', port=1. 'https://user:pw@sub.example.co.uk:8443/...' -> host='sub.example.co.uk', port=8443.

rules.rule: Degenerate '@' positions: an authority ending in '@' gives an empty host; an authority starting with '@' gives the whole rest as host.
STEP 6: the port is taken at the FIRST ':' of the post-userinfo authority (not the last). host = text before it, port-string = everything after it to the end of the authority.
rules.evidence: 'http://a:1:2' -> host='a', port=1 (last-colon parsing would give host='a:1', port=2). 'http://a:1:2/c' -> host='a', port=1, path='/c'. 'http://[::1]:8080/x' -> host='[', port=-1, path='/x' (first ':' is the one right after '['; no IPv6 bracket handling at all). 'http://[::1]/x' -> host='[', port=-1, path='/x'.

rules.rule: ANSWER TO (a): the port ':' search is strictly limited to the authority segment. A ':' after the first '/' (in the path) or after the first '?' (in the query) is NEVER mistaken for a port.
rules.evidence: 'http://a/b:c' -> http / a / -1 / '/b:c' / ''. 'http://a/b:1?c:2' -> http / a / -1 / '/b:1' / 'c:2'. 'http://a?b:1' -> http / a / -1 / '' / 'b:1'. 'http://a?b:1/c' -> http / a / -1 / '' / 'b:1/c'. 'http://a#b:1' -> http / a / -1 / '' / ''. 'http://a:1/2:3?4:5#6:7' -> http / a / 1 / '/2:3' / '4:5' (only the authority colon became a port).

rules.rule: The port-string is converted with a lenient stoi-style prefix parse (leading whitespace and '+' accepted, parsing stops at the first non-digit), then range-checked: a value outside 0..65535, or an unparsable/empty string, yields -1. An empty host with a valid port is allowed.
No percent-decoding happens anywhere before (or after) delimiter splitting: '%3F', '%23', '%2F', '%40', '%3A' stay literal and never act as delimiters.
rules.evidence: 'http://a%3Fb' -> host='a%3Fb', query=''. 'http://a%23b' -> host='a%23b'. 'http://a%2Fb' -> host='a%2Fb', path=''. 'http://a%40b' -> host='a%40b'. 'http://a%3A1' -> host='a%3A1', port=-1. 'http://a?b%23c' -> query='b%23c'.

rules.rule: Complete precedence order (fully determined): (1) truncate at first '#'; (2) split off query at first '?'; (3) find first '://' -> scheme (lowercased) or, if absent, whole remainder becomes path and host stays empty; (4) authority = up to first '/', path = from that '/' to end; (5) drop everything up to and including the first '@' in the authority; (6) split authority at first ':' -> host + lenient/range-checked port (-1 on failure). No step ever revisits an earlier one.
rules.evidence: Every probe is consistent. Worst-case check: 'http://a:1@b:2@c:3/d:4?e:5#f:6' -> scheme=http, host='b', port=2, path='/d:4', query='e:5'. Trace: strip '#f:6' -> split at '?' giving query 'e:5' -> '://' at 4 gives scheme http, rest 'a:1@b:2@c:3/d:4' -> authority 'a:1@b:2@c:3', path '/d:4' -> first '@' leaves 'b:2@c:3' -> first ':' gives host 'b', portstr '2@c:3' -> stoi -> 2.

rules.rule: FULL-FEATURED URL requested: 'https://user:pw@sub.example.co.uk:8443/a/b/c.html?x=1&y=2#frag' parses correctly and identically to RFC expectations.
rules.evidence: scheme='https', host='sub.example.co.uk', port=8443, path='/a/b/c.html', query='x=1&y=2' (fragment 'frag' discarded, not exposed). Also 'ftp://u:p@ftp.x.org:21/pub/f.txt?v=1#top' -> ftp / ftp.x.org / 21 / '/pub/f.txt' / 'v=1'.

rules.rule: Exit status is always 0 and exactly 5 newline-terminated lines are printed for every input tried, including the empty string; no input caused a throw or non-zero exit.
rules.evidence: '' -> ''/''/-1/''/'' with exit=0. Same for '?', '#', '/', ':', '@', '://', 'http://a:99999999999999999999/x' (out-of-range would throw from a bare stoi, so it is caught).

observations.note: (a) colon in path is NOT a port
(a) colon in query is NOT a port; empty path
only authority colon is a port
reverse order: query found, fragment cut
(d) userinfo with password stripped; port from post-@
userinfo colon is not a port
host stays empty; '/' NOT used to split
no IPv6 bracket handling; first ':' wins
DECISIVE: scheme would be 'a?' if '://' were found first
empty scheme still takes authority branch

uncertainties: Steps 1 and 2 ('#' truncation then '?' split) are indistinguishable from an equivalent formulation where the scheme search is performed globally but REJECTED if the '://' index is greater than the first '?'/'#' index. Every probe I designed (notably 'a?://b' -> path 'a', query '://b', and 'http://a#b?c' -> query '') is consistent with both; the observable 5-field behavior is identical, so I state the split-first model but the internal implementation could be either.

Because '#' is truncated globally and '?' is split globally before authority parsing, I could not construct any input where a '?' or '#' survives into the post-'://' remainder. So I cannot tell whether the authority-end scan is find('/') or find_first_of("/?#") — the two are behaviorally indistinguishable in this parser. I state find('/') because that is the minimal explanation.
Whether the fragment is stored anywhere (a fragment()/ref() accessor may exist on the class) is unobservable from this 5-line driver; all I can say is it never leaks into scheme/host/port/path/query.

The exact port-string acceptance predicate is inferred as "stoi-style prefix parse then 0..65535 range check". 'http://a:0x10' -> 0 and 'http://a: 1' -> 1 strongly imply std::stoi/strtol semantics, but I did not distinguish e.g. a manual isdigit loop with leading-whitespace skip and a '+' allowance, which would behave identically on every input I tried.
I did not determine whether the scheme lowercasing is locale-dependent or applies to non-ASCII bytes; only 'HTTP://A.COM/B?C' -> scheme 'http' was tested. Host case is definitely preserved ('A.COM').
No input produced a non-zero exit or missing line, but I did not probe non-UTF8 / embedded-NUL argv bytes, so I cannot rule out different delimiter behavior there.
